A **phaser** sweeps a few notches up and down the spectrum, and the result is a soft, swirling
"whoosh". It's the sound of the electric piano in a thousand 1970s records, and Eddie Van Halen's
guitar on the first Van Halen album.

**How to use the page.** The source starts as **chords**. The red line on the spectrum shows the
notches moving. Turn **Mix** to 100% and the effect disappears (to the ear), which says something
about how it works.

## The effect

<div class="sk" data-w="phaser" data-source="chords"></div>

## How it works

A phaser passes the sound through a chain of **all-pass filters**. An all-pass filter is a strange
kind of [filter](sound-filter.qmd): it doesn't change how loud any frequency is. It only delays some
frequencies more than others, so it shifts their **phase**. On its own you can't hear it.

But mix that phase-shifted copy back with the original, and wherever the copy has been shifted
exactly half a cycle the two cancel. Those cancellations are the **notches**. The stages here are
the browser's all-pass filters, each of which makes one notch, so **Stages** = 4 gives four notches. (A
guitar pedal uses simpler stages, and needs two of them per notch.) An [LFO](sound-lfo.qmd)
sweeps the all-pass filters up and down, and the notches sweep with them.

That's why the wet sound alone (Mix at 100%) sounds plain. The notches only exist when the shifted
copy meets the original. 50% gives the deepest notches.

## The controls

- **Stages**: more stages, more notches, a stronger effect. The MXR Phase 90 has two notches; 12 here
  is very dramatic.
- **Centre** and **Sweep**: where the notches sit and how far up and down they move.
- **Rate**: slow for a swirl, fast for a warble.
- **Width (Q)**: how sharp the phase change in each stage is, and so how narrow the notches are.
- **Feedback**: feeds the output back to the input; the areas between the notches turn into
  resonant peaks and the effect becomes more vocal and whistling. (The red line doesn't show the
  feedback.)

## Phaser or flanger?

Both sweep notches. A [flanger](sound-chorus.qmd) uses a short delay, which makes many evenly spaced
notches, like the teeth of a comb, so it sounds metallic and jet-like. A phaser uses all-pass
filters, which make a few notches that aren't evenly spaced, so it sounds softer and more liquid.
Switch the source to **noise** on both pages and compare the spectrum.
